verses.zh: 以色列年幼的时候，我爱他，就从埃及召出我的儿子来。
verses.en: “When Israel was a young man, I loved him like a son,[NOTE:1] and I summoned my son[NOTE:2] out of Egypt.
notes: The words “like a son” are not in the Hebrew text but are necessary to clarify what sort of love is intended (cf. also NLT).

The MT reads בְנִי (veni, “my son”); however, the LXX reflects בָנָיו (vanayv, “his sons”). The MT should be retained as original here because of internal evidence; it is much more appropriate to the context.
verses.commentary:
11:1-4 Hosea is characterized by its fresh and varied images to describe YHWH and
His actions. Two of the most powerful and personal are

- God as faithful lover, chapters 1-3

- God as loving parent (male and female), chapter 11

YHWH has revealed himself to fallen humanity by choosing things that humans
have experienced—deeply personal and powerfully moving things—and has said,
"I am like that to you." This is why family imagery and analogies are used so often in the Bible
in relation to God. All humans have experienced the deep feelings of human love and many have
experienced parenthood. Through these experiences God has clearly revealed himself and the
depth of His love and loyalty (cf. Hosea 11:8-9).

11:1 "When Israel was a youth I loved him" This is very similar in emphasis to
Hosea 9:10 and 10:1. It focuses on YHWH's love and choice of the descendants of Abraham
(cf. Deut. 4:32-40) in Egypt to uniquely be His people (cf. Amos 3:2, which reflects Exod. 19:5-6),
which was a prophetic fulfillment of Gen. 15:12-21.

YHWH chose a man to choose a family to choose a nation to represent and reveal Him
to the world (cf. Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6). Out of this family would come the Messiah (i.e. typological use
of this text in Matt. 2:15 in the life of Jesus).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HE CHOSE US

▣ "And out of Egypt I called My son" The term "son" in the singular in the
OT can refer to

- the nation of Israel (e.g. 1:10; Exod. 4:22)

- the King of Israel (e.g. 2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 2:7)

- the Messiah (e.g. Ps. 2:7, quoted in Acts 13:33; Heb. 1:5; 5:5)

This reference is used of Jesus as a child being taken to Egypt to protect Him from
Herod the Great in Matt. 2:15, however, in this context it refers to the nation of Israel.

Notice the emphasis on election, "I called" (BDB 894, KB 1128, Qal PERFECT).
In the OT election is primarily for service (Israel's place in YHWH's redemptive plan), while in the NT it is primarily for salvation (cf. Eph. 1:3-14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FATHERHOOD OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: "SONS OF. . ."

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION

verses.zh: 先知越发招呼他们，他们越发走开，向诸巴力献祭，给雕刻的偶像烧香。
verses.en: But the more I summoned[NOTE:1] them,the farther they departed from me.[NOTE:2] They sacrificed to the Baal idolsand burned incense to images.
notes: The MT reads קָרְאוּ (qareʾu, “they called”; Qal perfect third person common plural from קָרַא, qaraʾ, “to call”); cf. KJV and NASB; NIV11 “they were called.” However, the LXX and Syriac reflect כְּקָרְאִי (keqareʾi, “as I called”; preposition כְּ [kaf] + Qal infinitive construct from קָרַא + first person common singular suffix). The presence of the resumptive adverb כֵּן (ken, “even so”) in the following clause supports the alternate textual tradition reflected in the LXX and Syriac (cf. NAB, NIV84, NCV, NRSV, TEV, NLT).

The MT reads מִפְּנֵיהֶם (mippenehem, “from them”; preposition + masculine plural noun + third person masculine plural suffix); so KJV, ASV, and NASB. However, the LXX and Syriac reflect an alternate Hebrew textual tradition of מִפָּנַי הֵם (mippanay hem, “they [went away] from me”; preposition + masculine plural noun + first person common singular suffix, followed by third person masculine plural independent personal pronoun); cf. NAB, NIV, and NRSV. The textual variant was caused simply by faulty word division.
verses.commentary:
11:2 "they called them" This refers to the prophets (cf. LXX translation and 2 Kgs. 17:13-18; Isa. 6:10;
Jer. 7:25-26). However, Israel acted just like human teenagers. The more God called them (the Septuagint and the
Syriac have "I" instead of "they" in line one; and "Me" in line two), the more they did just the opposite (cf. Hosea 11:7b).

David A. Hubbard, Hosea (Tyndale OT Commentaries), redivides line 2
and thinks that "they" refers to tempters like the "Ba'al of Peor fertility-worshiping women of Num. 25. The lines would become
"the more they called them, The more they went from me" (p. 187). The Jerome Biblical Commentary asserts "they" refers to
all the local Ba'al altars (p. 262). To a wayward son, bent on self and sin, the call of idolatry was louder and stronger than the call
of a loving parent (i.e. Prodigal Son of Luke 15).

Whichever theory is true the settled wayward character is emphasized! Her past commitments are lost in her current desires.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "Ba'al" This refers to the male Canaanite fertility god who was called "Lord" and was the storm god in charge
of fertility. For a full discussion of the Canaanite pantheon see Archaeology and the Religion of Israel, by William Foxwell Albright.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "They kept sacrificing to the Baals,

And burning incense to idols" These two lines of poetry are parallel. Nothing is known of animal
sacrifices to Ba'al (JPSOA footnote, "calves"), therefore, the sacrifices (BDB 256, KB 261, Piel IMPERFECT)
may refer to offering incense (BDB 882, KB 1094, Piel IMPERFECT, cf. Isa. 65:7; Jer. 7:9; 18:15).

There was some sacrificing of children to Molech, the Phoenician fertility fire god. This may be referred to in Hosea
in some of the passages about the slaughter of children.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH

verses.zh: 我原教导以法莲行走，用膀臂抱着他们，他们却不知道是我医治他们。
verses.en: Yet it was I who led[NOTE:1] Ephraim;I took them by the arm,but they did not acknowledge that I had healed them.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “taught Ephraim to walk” (so ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV). The verb תִרְגַּלְתִּי (tirgalti, “I taught [him] to walk, I led [him]”; Tiphil perfect first person common singular from רָגַל, ragal, “to walk”) is an unusual verb stem: the Tiphil (properly Taphel) is attested three times in Biblical Hebrew (Hos 11:3; Jer 12:5; 22:15) and once in Biblical Aramaic (Ezra 4:7; see GKC 153 §55.h).
Or “that it was I who had healed them” (NIV and NLT are similar).
verses.commentary:
11:3 "it was I who taught Ephraim to walk" This is a rare VERB form (BDB 920, KB 1183,
Tiphel, PERFECT, the stem denotes causative action in the ACTIVE VOICE, similar to the
Hiphil stem) with an unusual meaning for the root ("foot"). Verses 3 and 4 show the love of God expressed in the analogy of YHWH
as a loving parent, both father and mother (emendation of Hosea 11:4b,c). The father either

- went before His child to walk

- went before His child in example and/or protection

SPECIAL TOPIC: FATHERHOOD OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

▣ "I took them in My arms" This is imagery of a loving parent, used of YHWH (cf. Deut. 1:31).

▣ "But they did not know that I healed them" Can you feel the pain of YHWH in this phrase? His own people,
who He saved out of Egypt and uniquely revealed Himself to, were attributing His love gifts to them as coming from the Canaanite
fertility gods! Wounded love!

The VERB "healed" (BDB 950, KB 1272, Qal PERFECT) is often used
for God forgiving sin, as seen in Hosea 5:13, 6:1; 7:1; Exod. 15:26; the parallelism of Ps. 163:3; and Isa. 1:5-6, examples of national sin
described in terms of a physical disease (also note Isa. 53:5 and 1 Pet. 2:24-25). Please look at the Special Topic below for a full discussion of this issue.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

verses.zh: 我用慈绳（慈：原文是人的）爱索牵引他们；我待他们如人放松牛的两腮夹板，把粮食放在他们面前。
verses.en: I drew them with leather cords,[NOTE:1]with straps of hide;[NOTE:2]I lifted the yoke[NOTE:3] from their neck[NOTE:4] and gently fed them.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “cords of human [kindness].” The noun אָדָם (ʾadam) is traditionally related to I אָדָם (“man”) and translated either literally or figuratively (as a metonymy of association for humane compassion): “cords of a man” (KJV, RSV margin, NASB), “cords of human kindness” (NIV, NCV), “human ties” (NJPS), and “cords of compassion” (RSV). But while it refers to humanity it rarely if ever means “humanely.” Another view sees the noun as II אָדָם (“leather”; HALOT 14 s.v. אָדָם) or possibly to be revocalized as אֹדֶם (ʾodem, “leather”; DCH rev. 1:153 s.v. אֹדֶם and 152 s.v. אָדָם II) and in parallel in this verse with II אַהֲבָה (ʾahavah, “leather”). This homonymic root is well attested in Arabic ʾadam (“skin”) and ʾadim (“tanned skin; leather”). It could fit the context of 11:4, which compares Israel to an animal: the Lord led him with leather cords, lifted the yoke from his neck, and fed him. Elsewhere, Hosea compares Israel to a stubborn cow (4:6) and harnessed heifer (10:11). It is somewhat common that the infrequent vocabulary of the Old Testament appears in poetic contexts, and this may be the case here. Richard S. Hess, “’ĀDĀM as ‘Skin’ and ‘Earth’: An Examination of Some Proposed Meanings in Biblical Hebrew,” TynBul (39) 1988: 141-42, claims that understanding the words as from the common roots is “acceptable for the context” and that taking the words as the more common roots is “the simplest and most suitable reading of the text.” HALOT cites Hans Walter Wolff for II אָדָם and II אַהֲבָה, but Hess notes that Wolff later rejected “leather” as a translation for these words in a commentary on Hosea. Hess is followed by NIDOTTE (261 s.v. אָדָם I).

Or “ropes of love.” The noun אַהֲבָה (ʾahava) is traditionally related to I אַהֲבָה (“love”; BDB 13 s.v. אַהֲבָה 2). This approach is adopted by most English translations: “bands of love” (KJV, RSV), “bonds of love” (NASB), “ties of love” (NIV), and “cords of love” (NJPS). However, אַהֲבָה could derive from the homonymic root II אַהֲבָה (“leather”; HALOT 18 s.v. II אַהֲבָה). This root is attested in Arabic and Ugaritic. It might occur in the description of Solomon’s sedan chair: “upholstered with purple linen, and inlaid with leather” (Song 3:10). The context of 11:4 compares Israel to a young heifer: the Lord could lead him with leather ropes, lift the yoke from his neck, and bend down to feed him. Elsewhere, Hosea compares Israel to a stubborn cow (4:6) and a young heifer harnessed for plowing (10:11). This may be supported by the parallelism with II אָדָם (ʾadam, “leather”; HALOT 14 s.v. II אָדָם). In addition, this could be an example of a homonymic wordplay on both roots: “ropes of leather/love.” For discussions of II אַהֲבָה, see G. R. Driver, “Supposed Arabisms in the Old Testament,” JBL 55 (1936): 111; G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 133; S. E. Loewenstamm, Thesaurus of the Language of the Bible, 1:39; and D. Grossberg, “Canticles 3:10 in the Light of a Homeric Analogue and Biblical Poetics,” BTB 11 (1981): 75-76. For homonymic wordplays, see W. G. E. Watson, Classical Hebrew Poetry [JSOTSup], 237-38, and J. Barr, Comparative Philology and the Text of the Old Testament, 151-55.

Heb “And I was to them like those who lift a yoke.” Eugen J. Pentiuc (Long-Suffering Love, 183, n. 940) says that the Vulgate and Syriac have the singular: “as one who lifts”). BHS suggests emending עֹל (‘ol, “yoke”) to עוּל (‘ul, “suckling”), and this might have originally required only a change of pointing: עֻל. Numerous commentaries and translations (NRSV, NJB, NIV11, NAB, CEB) have agreed. The NIV11 has, “like one who lifts a little child to the cheek.” J. Andrew Dearman (The Book of Hosea (NICOT), 283) notes that this is modern. The Latin and Syriac agree with the MT in the animal imagery. Cords and ropes suit animals. Embracing to the face is not otherwise attested in Scripture. Dearman sees parallels between Hos 11:1-4 and Exod 20:2-5, and the image can be removal of the yoke of slavery in Egypt (see Lev 26:13; Jer 2:20). A yoke was standard imagery for servitude (1 Kgs 12:4, 10-11, 14; Deut 28:48; Jer 28:14; 30:8). A harness on the jaws occurs in Isa 30:28. God’s feeding of Israel would have been in the wilderness. A yoke here would match imagery of a yoke in Hos 10:11. God removed Israel from slavery but will return it to slavery for its sin (10:11).
Heb “their jaws” (so KJV, ASV, NASB). This noun (לְחִי, lekhiy) can also mean “cheek,” which is how the NIV11, NRSV, NJB, NAB, and CEV take it here.
Heb “him.” This is regarded as a collective singular by most English versions and thus translated as a plural pronoun.
verses.commentary:
11:4 "with cords of a man, with bonds of love" This refers "to a child-training leash." YHWH's discipline is as much a sign of
His love as any of His mercy actions (cf. Heb. 12:5-13). Loving parental discipline is the key to understanding God's actions and
guidelines to sinful mankind, who are in the process of destroying themselves in the freedom and knowledge of "the tree of good and evil"
(cf. Gen. 3). He will not let us go unchallenged! He will not stand by and let us destroy ourselves.

It is possible that "cords of a man" could be translated "leather cords," from KB 14, II, cf. NET Bible, p. 1573, which
denoted tanned leather, from Arabic root for "skin."

▣ "as one who lifts the yoke from their jaws" The Hebrew term "yoke" (BDB 760) seems out of place in this context
(however, it could refer to Hosea 10:11). Yet, by changing a vowel and doubling the last consonant, it is possible to insert the Hebrew
term "infant" (BDB 760, cf. Hosea 14:1), which seems to fit the context of parental care much better (cf, NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 401). A possible
translation would be like the NEB, NAB, JB, NJB, "as one who lifts an infant to his cheek." This is possibly a reference to YHWH as a nursing mother
(cf. Isa. 49:15; 66:13; hear my sermon, "The Femininity of God" in the second green box on my homepage, sermon #111, www.freebiblecommentary.org.

God is not a male or female. He is an eternal, personal, spirit present throughout time, space, and all dimensions of reality.
He created male and female as a means of reproduction on this planet. He incorporates the best of both in Himself.

There are several places where this femininity is specific.

- Gen. 1:2, "brooded over the waters" ‒ this is a female bird word

- Hosea 1:4; Isa. 49:15; 66:9-13 ‒ God as a nursing mother

- The Arabic root, Shaddai means "a woman's breast."

verses.zh: 他们必不归回埃及地，亚述人却要作他们的王，因他们不肯归向我。
verses.en: They will return to Egypt![NOTE:1] Assyria will rule over them[NOTE:2] because they refuse to repent![NOTE:3]
notes: Or “Will they not return to Egypt?” (so NIV). Following the LXX and BHS, the MT לֹא (loʾ, “not”) should probably be read as לוֹ (lo, “to him”) and connected to the end of 11:4 rather than the beginning of 11:5. The textual confusion between לֹא and לוֹ probably reflects an unintentional scribal error due to a mistake in hearing (cf., e.g., Kethib/Qere in Ps 100:3).
Heb “Assyria, he will be his [Israel’s] king” (NASB similar).

Heb “return” (so KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV). The root שׁוּב (shuv, “to turn, return”) appears at the beginning and ending of this verse, creating an inclusio. This repetition produces an ironic wordplay: because Israel refuses to “return” to God or “turn” from its sin, it will “return” to Egypt. The punishment fits the crime.
verses.commentary:
11:5 "They will not return to the land of Egypt" This is a seeming contradiction to
Hosea 7:16; 8:13; 9:3. There are two possible theories of interpretation:

- Egypt is a symbol for slavery (see G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, p. 156).

- Egypt is another example of political alliances.

Theory 2 seems to fit the context of chapter 11:5 best, however, theory 1 seems to fit the context of the other biblical references better.

It is possible to translate "not" as "surely," this would solve the seeming contradiction (cf. RSV, NEB).

▣ "But Assyria-he will be their king" This is a clear prophecy of the Assyrian exile (cf. Hosea 7:11;
8:9-10; 9:3; 10:6). It is possible that the verse refers to rejecting Israel's trust in political alliances with both Egypt and Assyria. Assyria as
king may reflect 10:3. Israel wanted a king like the nations (cf. 1 Sam. 8:5); now they had one!

▣ "they refused to return to Me" The term "return" (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal INFINITIVE
CONSTRUCT) is the major OT root for repentance.

The pain of YHWH's heart can be seen in the VERB "refused" (BDB 549, KB 540, Piel
PERFECT). It was not ignorance on Israel's part for which they were culpable, but open-eyed rebellion against YHWH and
His law (cf. Hosea 7:13-15; 8:1,12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

verses.zh: 刀剑必临到他们的城邑，毁坏门闩，把人吞灭，都因他们随从自己的计谋。
verses.en: A sword will flash in their cities;it will destroy the bars of their city gates,and will devour them in their fortresses.
verses.commentary:
11:6 "The sword will whirl against their cities" The VERB (BDB 296, KB 297, Qal PERFECT with waw) is used of

- dancing

- the turbulence of storms

- writhing in the pain of childbirth

- Here it is the flashing, whirling action of a personified sword (cf. Isa. 34:5,6; Ezek. 21) as it devastates the cities of Israel.

▣ "gate bars" This term (BDB 94 II, #3) refers to

- the wooden beams used to secure city gates at night (Israel was trusting in
her fortifications, cf. Hosea 8:14; 10:14)

- to divination (KB 109 V, "oracle priest," cf. Isa. 44:25; Jer. 50:36) and as parallel to "counsel" (i.e. Hosea 10:6; also note
Isa. 30:2; Jer. 7:24)

▣ "because of their counsels" This could refer to

- the policies of Jeroboam I, who set up the golden calves

- the ongoing policies of the different royal Israeli dynasties who succeeded him

- the decision of political advisors. This is referred to several times in Hosea
(e.g. Hosea 7:12)

verses.zh: 我的民偏要背道离开我；众先知虽然招呼他们归向至上的主，却无人尊崇主。
verses.en: My people are obsessed[NOTE:1] with turning away from me;[NOTE:2] they call to Baal,[NOTE:3] but he will never exalt them!
notes: The term תְלוּאִים (teluʾim, Qal passive participle masculine plural from תָּלָא, talaʾ, “to hang”) literally means “[My people] are hung up” (BDB 1067 s.v. תָּלָא). The verb תָּלָא // תָּלָה (“to hang”) is often used in a concrete sense to describe hanging an item on a peg (Ps 137:2; Song 4:4; Isa 22:24; Ezek 15:3; 27:10) or impaling the body of an executed criminal (Gen 40:19, 22; 41:13; Deut 21:22, 23; Josh 8:29; 10:26; 2 Sam 21:12; Esth 2:23; 5:14; 6:4; 7:9, 10; 8:7; 9:13, 14, 25). It is used figuratively here to describe Israel’s moral inability to detach itself from apostasy. Several English versions capture the sense well: “My people are bent on turning away from me” (RSV, NASB), “My people are determined to turn from me” (NIV), “My people are determined to reject me” (CEV; NLT “desert me”), “My people persist in its defection from me” (NJPS), and “they insist on turning away from me” (TEV).
The first person common singular suffix on the noun מְשׁוּבָתִי (meshuvati; literally, “turning of me”) functions as an objective genitive: “turning away from me.”

The meaning and syntax of the MT is enigmatic: וְאֶל־עַל יִקְרָאֻהוּ (veʾel ʾal yiqraʾuhu, “they call upwards to him”). Many English versions, including KJV, NIV, NRSV, and NLT, take the referent of “him” as the “Most High.” The BHS editors suggest reading וְאֶל־בַּעַל יִקְרָא וְהוּא (veʾel baʿal yiqraʾ vehuʾ, “one calls to Baal, but he…”), connecting the third person masculine singular independent personal pronoun וְהוּא (vehuʾ, “but he…”) with the following clause. The early Greek recensions (Aquila and Symmachus), as well as the Aramaic Targum and the Vulgate, vocalized עֹל (ʿol) as “yoke” (as in 11:4): “they cry out because of [their] yoke” (a reading followed by TEV).
verses.commentary:
11:7 "So My people are bent on turning from Me" The VERB (BDB 1067, KB 1736, Qal
PASSIVE PARTICIPLE), which is used literally in Deut. 28:66, "to hang something before someone," here is
imagery for a tendency or natural leaning toward someone/something (but not YHWH).

The term "turning from" (BDB 1000) means to "turn back" or "apostatize" (cf. Hosea 14:5; in Jer. 3:6)

- of Israel, in Jer. 2:18; 3:22; 5:6; 8:5; 14:7

- of Judah, often translated "faithless"

- Instead of turning to God in repentance they turned away from Him in apostasy!

The opening "My people" is an allusion to Hosea 1:9 (i.e. "Lo-Ammi"), but with the future hope of the full
hope of Hosea 2:23 (i.e. Ruhamah, cf. Hosea 1:6 and Ammi)!

▣

NASB
"they call them to the One on high"

NKJV, NRSV
"they call on the Most High"

NJB
"if they are summoned to come up"

REB
"they call in unison to Ba'al"

JPSOA
"When it is summoned upward"

Peshitta
"they shall call to God"

NET
"they call to Ba'al"

The MT has "upwards they call it altogether." The question is, who does line b refer to and who does
line c refer to? Possibly

- line b refers to Ba'al

- line c refers to

- YHWH (NASB, NKJV, Peshitta)

- Ba'al (REB, NET)

Several ancient Greek translations, the Aramaic Targums, and
the Latin Vulgate, take the word "upward" (BDB 752) as "yoke" (BDB 760).

- upwards ‒ על

- yoke ‒ על (cf. v. 4)

"They will cry out because of the yoke that is on them, but no one will lift it" (TEV).

▣ "None at all exalts Him" This is the problem of fallen mankind,
especially the covenant people (e.g. Isa. 53:6 a,b, quoted in the NT by Peter in 1 Pet. 2:25).

verses.zh: 以法莲哪，我怎能舍弃你？以色列啊，我怎能弃绝你？我怎能使你如押玛？怎能使你如洗扁？我回心转意，我的怜爱大大发动。
verses.en: “How can I give you up,[NOTE:1] O Ephraim?How can I surrender you, O Israel?How can I treat you like Admah?How can I make you like Zeboyim?I have had a change of heart.[NOTE:2] All my tender compassions are aroused.[NOTE:3]
notes: The imperfect verbs in 11:8 function as imperfects of capability. See IBHS 564 §34.1a.

The phrase נֶהְפַּךְ עָלַי לִבִּי (nehpakh ʿalay libbi) is an idiom that can be taken in two ways: (1) a tumult of emotions, not just a clash of ideas, that are afflicting a person (Lam 1:20; HALOT 253 s.v. הפך 1.c) and (2) a decisive change of policy, that is, a reversal of sentiment from amity to hatred (Exod 14:5; Ps 105:25; BDB 245 s.v. הָפַךְ 1; HALOT 253 s.v. 3). Some English versions express God’s emotional discomfort and tension over the prospect of destroying Israel: “mine heart is turned within me” (KJV), “my heart recoils within me” (RSV, NRSV), “My heart is turned over within Me” (NASB), and “My heart is torn within me” (NLT). Others stress volitional reversal of a previous decision to totally destroy Israel: “I have had a change of heart” (NJPS), “my heart is changed within me” (NIV), and “my heart will not let me do it!” (TEV). Both BDB 245 s.v. 1.b and HALOT 253 s.v. 3 suggest that the idiom describes a decisive change of heart (reversal of decision to totally destroy Israel once and for all) rather than God’s emotional turbulence, shifting back and forth between whether to destroy or spare Israel. This volitional nuance is supported by the modal function of the first person common singular imperfects in 11:8 (“I will not carry out my fierce anger…I will not destroy Ephraim…I will not come in wrath”) and by the prophetic announcement of future restoration in 11:10-11. Clearly, a dramatic reversal both in tone and in divine intention occurs between 11:5-11.

The Niphal of כָּמַר (kamar) means “to grow warm, tender” (BDB 485 s.v. כָּמַר), as its use in a simile with an oven demonstrates (Lam 5:10). It is used several times to describe the arousal of the most tender affection (Gen 43:30; 1 Kgs 3:26; Hos 11:8; BDB 485 s.v. 1; HALOT 482 s.v. כמר 1). Cf. NRSV “my compassion grows warm and tender.”
verses.commentary:
11:8 "How can I give you up" The heart of YHWH is breaking (cf. third set of parallel lines in this verse,
cf. Hosea 6:4) as His rebellious child turns away from a loyal loving parent. In the OT a child like this could be stoned to
death (cf. Deut. 21:18-21). How or where do justice and love meet? (i.e. in the Messiah!)

▣ "How can I surrender you" This VERB (BDB 171, KB 545, Piel IMPERFECT)
means "to deliver up" or "give over." This word is used only three times in the OT and only in Gen. 14:20 with a similar meaning.

▣ "Admah. . .Zeboiim" These are cities of the Plain which were destroyed for their wickedness along with Sodom
and Gomorrah (cf. Gen. 10:19; 19:24-25; Deut. 29:23). They no longer existed; YHWH must judge Israel, but not to extinction.

▣ "My heart is turned over within Me" This VERB (BDB 245, KB 253, Niphal
PERFECT) is the general word for "to turn" or "overturn." It is used to describe God's overthrow of the cities
of the Plain (alluded to in the previous two parallel lines of Hosea 11:8) in Gen. 19:21,25,29; Deut. 29:22. It is not that God has changed
His anger toward Israel's sin and rebellion, but that His love and mercy will provide a future salvation. This is the essence of the new
covenant of Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36, which is based on the character of YHWH, the work of the Messiah, and the wooing of the Spirit,
not human performance of an external code. God has changed His ways of dealing with fallen humanity (i.e. divine performance vs. human
obedience to an external law code, cf. a second possible meaning of the VERB, TEV, NIV, NET Bible).

▣ "All My compassions are kindled" This term for "compassions" (BDB 637) is used in only three places in the
OT, see Isa. 57:18; Zech. 1:13; and here.

The VERB "kindled" (BDB 485, KB 481, Niphal PERFECT) means "to grow warm
or tender," and was originally used of heating fruit in the ground to ripen it (e.g. Gen. 43:30; 1 Kgs 3:26; and here).

verses.zh: 我必不发猛烈的怒气，也不再毁灭以法莲。因我是　神，并非世人，是你们中间的圣者；我必不在怒中临到你们。
verses.en: I cannot carry out[NOTE:1] my fierce anger!I cannot totally destroy Ephraim!Because I am God, and not man—the Holy One among you—I will not come in wrath!
notes: The three imperfect verbs function as imperfects of capability, similar to the imperfects of capability in 11:8. See IBHS 564 §34.1a.
verses.commentary:
11:9 "I will not execute My fierce anger" The CONSTRUCT "fierce anger" (BDB 354 and 60) is also found in

- Hosea 8:5, e.g. Exod. 32:12 at the golden calf of Aaron

- Num. 25:4 at Israel's idolatry at Shittim

- Num. 32:13-15 at Israel's lack of faith about entering the Promised Land

- Josh. 7:26 at Achan's sin at Ai; Deut. 13:17 at idolatry of a city and many more

▣ "I will not destroy Ephraim again" YHWH chooses to have mercy (cf. Jer. 26:3). But this does not mean that
they were not punished (cf. Hosea 11:10a; Jer. 30:11). Sin always has consequences in time and eternity.

▣ "For I am God" This is the general name for deity in the ANE, El (BDB 42 II).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, A.

▣ "not man" This should go without saying (cf. Num. 23:19; 1 Sam. 15:29; Job 9:32), but sometimes the physicalness
of God is asserted as the meaning of "image and likeness" in Gen. 1:26-27.

- God is spirit!

- God is holy (this context is the only place in Hosea that this characteristic is attributed to YHWH, cf. Hosea 11:12).

- He was active in physical creation, but not part of it.

▣ "the Holy One in your midst" This (BDB 899, 872) is similar in meaning to the term, "Immanuel" which means
"God with us" (BDB 769, cf Isa. 6:12; Isa. 7:14). The Bible begins with God and His highest creation, humans, in a garden (cf. Genesis 1-2)
together and ends with God and humans in a garden together (cf. Revelation 21-22).

The essence of biblical faith is God and His highest creation in fellowship, not only spiritually but physically. Humans were
created for fellowship with God (cf. Gen. 1:26-27). There was never meant to be a transcendent and immanent distinction. Only human sin caused the need!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

▣

This ambiguous Hebrew phrase can be understood in several ways
depending on the Hebrew root:

- "to burn" or "to consume" (BDB 128)

- "to remove" or "to destroy" (BDB 128)

- "with" plus "agitation" or "wrath" (BDB 786)

- MT, "and I will not enter the city" (VERB BDB 97, KB 112;
OBJECT, Qal IMPERFECT and the
BDB 746 II), which would link it to Hosea 8:14; 10:14

YHWH's presence demanded judgment

verses.zh: 耶和华必如狮子吼叫，子民必跟随他。他一吼叫，他们就从西方急速而来。
verses.en: “He will roar like a lion, and they will follow the Lord;when he roars, his children will come trembling[NOTE:1] from the west.
notes: When the verb חָרַד (kharad, “to tremble”) is used with prepositions of direction, it denotes “to go or come trembling” (BDB 353 s.v. חָרַד 4; e.g., Gen 42:28; 1 Sam 13:7; 16:4; 21:2; Hos 11:10, 11). Thus, the phrase מִיָּם…וְיֶחֶרְדוּ (veyekheredu…miyyam) means “to come trembling from the west” (cf. NAB “shall come frightened from the west”).
verses.commentary:
11:10 "He will roar like a lion" "Roar" here does not refer to an act of violence on the part of a wild animal, but a parent calling little ones home.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

▣ "And His sons will come trembling from the west" There may be a word sound play between YHWH's
"fierce anger" (BDB 354) and "they will come trembling" (BDB 353, KB 350, Qal IMPERFECT, used twice,
cf. Hosea 10:11). This term is used

- in Gen. 42:28 at fear over an act of God

- in 1 Sam. 10:4 at fearful respect of God's prophet

- in 1 Sam. 21:1 as fear in the presence of King David

The ADJECTIVE is used of awe and reverence at God's word in Isa. 66:2; Ezra 9:4; 10:3.

The direction of the coming "west" (literally "the sea") is surprising since Assyria is to the east. Some
scholars see Hosea 11:10 and 11 as a return from three directions (i.e. from everywhere, cf. Isa. 11:11-12).

- the islands and coast land at Palestine, Hosea 11:10

- Egypt, Hosea 11:11

- Assyria, Hosea 11:11

verses.zh: 他们必如雀鸟从埃及急速而来，又如鸽子从亚述地来到。我必使他们住自己的房屋。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: They will return in fear and trembling[NOTE:1] like birds from Egypt,like doves from Assyria,and I will settle them in their homes,” declares the Lord.
notes: For the meaning of חָרַד (harad, “to tremble”) with prepositions of direction, see 11:10 above.
verses.commentary:
11:11 "They will come. . .from Egypt. . .from the land of Assyria" Many of the covenant people fled Egypt during
the Neo-Babylonian invasion and exile. God will bring His people home!

▣ "I will settle them in their houses" This is a reference to one of the promises of YHWH mentioned in
the cursing and blessing section of Deuteronomy 27 and 28.

verses.zh: 以法莲用谎话，以色列家用诡计围绕我；犹大却靠　神掌权，向圣者有忠心（或译：犹大向　神，向诚实的圣者犹疑不定）。
verses.en: (12:1)[NOTE:1] Ephraim has surrounded me with lies;the house of Israel has surrounded me[NOTE:2] with deceit.But Judah still roams about with[NOTE:3] God;he remains faithful to the Holy One.
notes: Beginning with 11:12, the verse numbers through 12:14 in the English Bible differ by one from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (BHS), with 11:12 ET = 12:1 HT, 12:1 ET = 12:2 HT, etc., through 12:14 ET = 12:15 HT. From 13:1 to 13:16 the verse numbers in the English Bible and the Hebrew Bible are again the same.

The phrase “has surrounded me” is not repeated in the Hebrew text here but is implied by the parallelism in the preceding line. It is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons, smoothness, and readability.

The verb רוּד (rud, “to roam about freely”) is used in a concrete sense to refer to someone wandering restlessly and roaming back and forth (BDB 923 s.v. רוּד; Judg 11:37). Here, it is used figuratively, possibly with positive connotations, as indicated by the preposition עִם (ʿim, “with”), to indicate accompaniment: “but Judah still goes about with God” (HALOT 1194 s.v. רוד). Some English versions render it positively: “Judah still walks with God” (RSV, NRSV), “but Judah stands firm with God” (NJPS), and “but Judah yet ruleth with God” (KJV, ASV). Other English versions adopt the negative connotation “to wander restlessly” and nuance עִם in an adversative sense (“against”): “Judah is still rebellious against God” (NAB), “Judah is restive under God” (REB), “Judah is unruly against God” (NIV), and “the people of Judah are still rebelling against me” (TEV).
verses.commentary:
11:12 The Masoretic Text lists verse 12 with chapter 12. Context confirms this! The last phrase of verse 12 is one
of the central passages of the entire book (cf. Hosea 6:6; 8:7). It emphasizes YHWH's faithfulness and Israel's faithlessness.
This is the tension between an unconditional (God's character) and conditional covenant (human obedience).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "Ephraim surrounds Me with lies" The VERB (BDB 685, KB 738, Qal
PERFECT) was used earlier in Hosea 7:2, where Israel's evil deeds surround them.

Israel's lies could be (cf. Hosea 7:13)

- covenant violations (broken promises)

- political counsel (foreign alliances, 7:3)

- religious divination (idol-priests)

- false prophets (prosperity and security)

- false information about YHWH

▣

NASB
"Judah is also unruly against God"

NKJV, NRSV
"Judah still walks with God"

TEV
"the people of Judah are still rebelling against me"

NJB
"(But Judah still is on God's side)"

The Hebrew is ambiguous. The question remains, "Are the last two poetic lines in parallel or
in contrast?" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY) Is Judah
contrasted with a sinful Israel (JPSOA) or are Judah and Israel contrasted with a faithful Holy God (cf. Hosea 12:2)?

Some scholars see the VERB as "wander" or "roam" (BDB 923, e.g. Hiphil,
PERFECT, Gen. 27:40; Qal, Jer. 2:31); others see it as (BDB 921, Qal PERFECT,
Isa. 14:2; Ezek. 34:4; Hiphil PERFECT, Isa. 41:2).

▣ "the Holy One who is faithful" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE
and SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT
